title: Prohibition of the Use of Force and Non-Intervention

slides.title: The Charter as a constitution
slides.text: The table asks what a constitution does and finds each function in the Charter. Principles and values: Articles 1 and 2, the purposes and principles. Institutional structure: five principal organs with differing tasks and powers. Law-making: Article 38 of the ICJ Statute. Law enforcement: Chapter VII, the Security Council's economic, financial and non-military sanctions and its authorizations to use force. And a hierarchy of norms: Article 103, under which Charter obligations prevail over obligations under any other international agreement — the international counterpart of a constitution outranking ordinary statutes.

cards.q: In what sense is the UN Charter a constitution in the material sense?
cards.a: It supplies principles and values (Arts 1-2), an institutional structure (the principal organs), law-making (via Art 38 ICJ Statute), law enforcement (Chapter VII), and a hierarchy of norms (Art 103, Charter obligations prevailing over other agreements).

slides.title: Section: the basic principles
slides.text: A divider: what follows are the 'constitutional' principles of the international legal order.

slides.title: How the prohibition of force was built
slides.text: Start with the distinction that organises the whole field: ius ad bellum asks WHEN force may be used, ius in bello HOW it must be conducted. In the nineteenth and early twentieth century there was no ius ad bellum limitation at all — war was part of a state's external sovereignty — while the rules of ius in bello grew, the 'humanization' of war. Then three steps: the League of Nations in 1919 imposed a relative prohibition with a three-month cooling-off period; the Briand-Kellogg Pact of 1928 declared war no means of policy; and the UN Charter finally imposed a comprehensive prohibition of the use of force with exactly two exceptions — self-defence and collective security.

terms.def: The law on when force may lawfully be used.
The law governing how hostilities must be conducted; international humanitarian law.

cards.q: Distinguish ius ad bellum from ius in bello, and say why the distinction matters.
cards.a: Ius ad bellum governs when force may be used, ius in bello how it is conducted. They are independent: a state fighting unlawfully must still obey humanitarian law, and a lawful defender is equally bound.

cards.q: Trace the three steps from unlimited war to the comprehensive prohibition of force.
cards.a: League of Nations 1919: a relative prohibition with a three-month cooling-off period. Briand-Kellogg Pact 1928: war renounced as a means of policy. UN Charter: a comprehensive prohibition with two exceptions, self-defence and collective security.

slides.title: The reach of the Briand-Kellogg Pact
slides.text: A map of the 1928 Pact's signatories, distinguishing initial and subsequent signatories, the colonies and dependent territories of signatories, and League of Nations mandate territories assigned to them. The colouring shows how much of the world was covered indirectly — through colonies rather than through consent.

slides.title: Article 2(4) dissected
slides.text: Four readings that the wording forces. It prohibits actual force, not merely war — so an undeclared operation counts. It prohibits the THREAT of force as well as its use. 'Force' means military or armed force; economic force is NOT included, which is why sanctions are analysed under non-intervention instead. And it covers aggression, invasion, aerial bombardment, military occupation, and the indirect use of force — sending armed bands to carry out military force abroad. The only exceptions are Article 51 self-defence and Chapter VII measures of the Security Council.

terms.def: Sending or substantially involving armed bands or irregulars to carry out force abroad.

cards.q: State A imposes a crushing economic embargo on State B. Does that breach Article 2(4)?
cards.a: No. 'Force' in Article 2(4) means military or armed force; economic pressure falls outside it. The right question is whether the embargo amounts to prohibited intervention through coercion.

cards.q: Name four forms of conduct covered by the prohibition in Article 2(4).
cards.a: Aggression; invasion and aerial bombardment; military occupation; and the indirect use of force by sending armed bands abroad. The threat of force is equally prohibited.

slides.title: Section: self-defence
slides.text: A divider introducing the first exception.

slides.title: The conditions of self-defence
slides.text: Run these in order in any case. First, an ARMED ATTACK — and against a member state, not merely against individual persons. Second, timing: the attack must have occurred or be continuing; anticipatory or pre-emptive self-defence is at most admissible against an IMMINENT threat. Third, NECESSITY — could the attack be averted without military means? Self-defence has no punitive function, so retaliation is not self-defence. Fourth, PROPORTIONALITY, measured against the prior armed attack by means, methods, weapons and scale; disproportionate force is itself an unlawful use of force. Finally the two forms: individual, exercised by the victim state, and collective, exercised by others at the victim's request, either ad hoc or in advance through an alliance such as NATO.

terms.def: The threshold condition for Art 51 self-defence; more than a mere frontier incident or minor use of force.
Defence of the victim state by others, lawful only upon the victim's request.

cards.q: State B suffers an armed attack; three weeks after it ends, B bombs the attacker's capital. Lawful self-defence?
cards.a: No. Self-defence requires an occurring or continuing attack and must be necessary to avert it; it has no punitive function. A response after the attack has ended is retaliation, not self-defence, and is itself an unlawful use of force.

cards.q: May a third state use force in defence of a victim state on its own initiative?
cards.a: No. Collective self-defence is lawful only upon the victim state's request — whether made ad hoc or in advance through an alliance.

cards.q: List the conditions for lawful self-defence under Article 51.
cards.a: An armed attack against a state; the attack occurring or continuing (anticipatory defence only against an imminent attack); necessity — no non-military means available; and proportionality to the attack.

slides.title: Self-defence against non-state actors
slides.text: The hard question. Article 51 does not on its face limit the source of the attack, which is the argument for allowing self-defence against terrorist groups. Against it stands the ICJ's Wall opinion of 2004: Article 51 recognises an inherent right of self-defence in the case of armed attack by ONE STATE AGAINST ANOTHER, and Israel did not claim the attacks were imputable to a foreign state. The Court thus read a state-attribution requirement into the provision — a position much criticised since 2001 but still the ICJ's.

cards.q: Can a state invoke Article 51 self-defence against an armed attack by a non-state group?
cards.a: Contested. The text does not limit the source of the attack, but the ICJ in the Wall opinion (2004) read Article 51 as covering armed attack by one state against another and required attribution to a state. State practice since 2001 pulls the other way — give both sides.

slides.title: Collective security: the Council's competence
slides.text: Chapter VII covers action with respect to threats to the peace, breaches of the peace and acts of aggression. Article 24 confers on the Security Council PRIMARY responsibility and says it acts ON BEHALF of the members — with the open question whether the General Assembly has a subsidiary competence, the claim made by the Uniting for Peace resolution of 1950. Article 39 supplies the three triggers, and Article 25 the binding force: members agree to accept and carry out the Council's decisions. Note the interpretive point on the slide: reading Council resolutions is not the same exercise as reading a treaty under Article 31 VCLT — literal and historical interpretation carry more weight.

terms.def: GA resolution asserting a subsidiary competence of the Assembly to recommend collective measures where the Council is blocked by a veto.
The Council determines the existence of a threat to the peace, breach of the peace or act of aggression — the gateway to Chapter VII.

cards.q: What must the Security Council determine before it can act under Chapter VII, and where is that?
cards.a: The existence of a threat to the peace, a breach of the peace or an act of aggression — Article 39, the gateway to all Chapter VII measures.

cards.q: The Council is blocked by a veto. Can the General Assembly act instead?
cards.a: Contested. The Uniting for Peace resolution of 1950 asserts a subsidiary competence for the Assembly to recommend collective measures, but the Assembly can only recommend, not bind, and Article 12 limits it while the Council is seised.

slides.title: Non-military measures under Article 41
slides.text: Article 40 allows provisional measures to prevent the situation deteriorating; Article 41 then allows binding NON-military measures. The range is far wider than the word 'sanctions' suggests: export and import embargoes, sectoral measures on arms or oil, restrictions on communication and transport; targeted sanctions against individuals — asset freezes, travel bans, bans on trading in natural resources such as blood diamonds; and a set of measures that look like legislation — creating ad hoc criminal tribunals, imposing duties to prosecute or extradite (Lockerbie), imposing a settlement (Dayton 1995), general obligations to fight terrorism, boundary delimitations (Kuwait-Iraq 1991), prohibitions on weapons of mass destruction, compensation commissions, and international territorial administrations in East Timor and Kosovo. The slide's own phrase for this is the quasi-legislative powers of the Council.

terms.def: Measures aimed at named individuals or entities — asset freezes, travel bans — rather than at a whole economy.

cards.q: Give three examples of Article 41 measures that go beyond classic economic sanctions.
cards.a: Creating ad hoc criminal tribunals (ICTY, ICTR); imposing obligations to prosecute or extradite (Lockerbie); delimiting a boundary (Kuwait-Iraq 1991); establishing territorial administrations (East Timor, Kosovo); imposing general counter-terrorism duties.

slides.title: Military measures: Articles 42 and 43
slides.text: Article 42 lets the Council take action by air, sea or land forces where Article 41 measures would be or have proved inadequate. Article 43 was to supply the means: members undertake to make forces available under special agreements. Those agreements were NEVER concluded, so the Council has no standing army — and the practice developed a 'second best option': AUTHORIZATIONS to member states to use force, phrased as 'all necessary means', as in Iraq-Kuwait 1991 and Libya 2011 for the protection of civilians. Peacekeeping forces developed alongside.

terms.def: The standard formula by which the Council authorizes member states to use force on its behalf.

cards.q: Why does the Security Council authorize states to use force rather than using forces of its own?
cards.a: Because the Article 43 special agreements placing national forces at the Council's disposal were never concluded. The practice substituted authorizations to member states, formulated as 'all necessary means'.

slides.title: Peacekeeping: legal basis and conditions
slides.text: No Charter provision creates peacekeeping, so its basis is threefold: implied powers, as held in Certain Expenses; an argument a maiore ad minus from Chapter VII — if the Council may authorize force, it may do less; and customary law and the practice of the Organization. The classical conditions: a Security Council resolution in the form of a recommendation, military command with the Council through the Military Staff Committee, partly voluntary funding, the CONSENT of the parties to the conflict where those are states, and by convention no participation by the five permanent members.

cards.q: On what legal bases does UN peacekeeping rest?
cards.a: Implied powers (Certain Expenses), an a maiore ad minus argument from Chapter VII, and customary law and the practice of the Organization — the Charter itself does not mention peacekeeping.

slides.title: How peacekeeping mandates grew
slides.text: The classical mandate stabilized a provisional ceasefire: separating the forces, monitoring implementation, with impartiality and a purely defensive use of force for self-protection. The mandate then extended — police tasks, securing areas, protecting civilians, humanitarian assistance, civil administration and justice, protecting elections — and with it two of the classical conditions fell away: consent of the conflicting parties is no longer always required, and armed force may be used actively to protect civilians and humanitarian assistance. The slide ends with a question mark over 'peace enforcement', which is precisely the point at which peacekeeping stops being peacekeeping.

cards.q: What distinguishes classical peacekeeping from robust modern mandates?
cards.a: Classical peacekeeping required the parties' consent, impartiality and force only in self-defence. Modern mandates may operate without consent and authorize active force to protect civilians and humanitarian assistance — approaching peace enforcement.

slides.title: Responsibility to protect
slides.text: The World Summit Outcome of 2005, paragraphs 138 and 139, and the two paragraphs do different jobs. Paragraph 138 places the responsibility on EACH STATE to protect its own population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity — four crimes, no more. Paragraph 139 places a responsibility on the international community: first to use peaceful means under Chapters VI and VIII, and then, should peaceful means be inadequate and national authorities be MANIFESTLY FAILING, to take collective action through the SECURITY COUNCIL, in accordance with the Charter including Chapter VII, case by case. R2P therefore creates no new right to use force outside the Council — that is its most commonly misunderstood feature.

terms.def: Responsibility to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity (World Summit Outcome 2005, paras 138-139).

cards.q: Does R2P authorize a state to use force to stop atrocities without Security Council approval?
cards.a: No. Paragraph 139 channels collective action through the Security Council in accordance with the Charter. R2P creates no new exception to Article 2(4).

cards.q: Which four crimes does R2P cover?
cards.a: Genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity.

slides.title: The prohibition of intervention
slides.text: The Friendly Relations Declaration of 1970 states it in three movements. No state or group of states has the right to intervene, directly or indirectly, for any reason whatever, in the internal or external affairs of another. No state may use or encourage economic, political or any other measures to COERCE another state in order to obtain the subordination of the exercise of its sovereign rights or to secure advantages; nor organize, assist, foment, finance, incite or tolerate subversive, terrorist or armed activities directed at the violent overthrow of another state's regime, or interfere in civil strife. And every state has an inalienable right to choose its political, economic, social and cultural systems without interference.

slides.title: Nicaragua on what makes intervention unlawful
slides.text: Paragraph 209 supplies the test in two parts. The principle protects matters in which each state is permitted by sovereignty to decide FREELY — the choice of political, economic, social and cultural system and the formulation of foreign policy. And intervention is wrongful when it uses methods of COERCION in regard to those choices. Coercion is, in the Court's words, the element which defines and indeed forms the very essence of prohibited intervention. So the two-step test is: a matter within the state's free choice, plus coercion.

terms.def: The defining element of unlawful intervention: pressure depriving the target state of free choice in a matter reserved to it.

cards.q: What is the two-part test for unlawful intervention under Nicaragua?
cards.a: The matter must be one the target state is free to decide by virtue of sovereignty — its political, economic, social and cultural system and its foreign policy — and the conduct must use methods of coercion in regard to that choice.

slides.title: Nicaragua on intervention by invitation
slides.text: Paragraph 246 answers a question that recurs in every civil war. Intervention at the request of the GOVERNMENT is already allowable; the Court holds that it would destroy the principle if intervention were also allowed at the request of an OPPOSITION group, because then any state could intervene at any moment, on one side or the other. So invitation by the recognised government can justify intervention; invitation by rebels cannot.

cards.q: An opposition movement invites a foreign state to intervene in its country's civil war. Lawful?
cards.a: No. Nicaragua para 246: intervention at the request of the government is allowable, but allowing it at the request of the opposition would leave nothing of the principle of non-intervention.

slides.title: Where the line runs, with examples
slides.text: Substance: no intervening in another state's internal affairs, and no exerting pressure to obtain advantages to which one is not entitled — all BELOW the threshold of armed force, which is Article 2(4)'s territory. Examples given as covered: subversive intervention against a government, support for the political opposition (Nicaragua), influencing another country's political decision-making such as Russian interference in the 2016 US elections, and secondary sanctions like the US measures on Iran and Nord Stream. Examples given as NOT covered: refusing development aid for political reasons, unilaterally terminating economic cooperation, and providing purely humanitarian assistance — the last on condition of impartiality.

terms.def: Measures penalising third-state persons for dealing with the primary target; contested as coercive intervention.

cards.q: State A stops its development aid to State B to punish B's government. Is that prohibited intervention?
cards.a: No. Withholding aid one is not obliged to give, and terminating voluntary economic cooperation, are not coercion in the Nicaragua sense — no legal entitlement of B is being overridden.

cards.q: Is covert interference in another state's elections unlawful, and under which rule?
cards.a: Yes — as prohibited intervention, not as a use of force. It coerces or manipulates a matter (the political system and decision-making) that sovereignty reserves to the target state's free choice.
